newsitem.title: PERU: Castro formally agrees to take in Peru rebels.
newsitem.headline: Castro formally agrees to take in Peru rebels.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro formally agreed to take in Peru's Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima for three months, Japan Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Thursday.

Hashimoto was speaking in Tokyo after a Japanese envoy delivered a personal appeal to Castro in Havana from the prime minister asking for asylum for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels on humanitarian grounds.
"I hope this will accelerate moves to seek an early solution," Hashimoto told reporters in Tokyo.
Japanese government sources in Tokyo said Castro told the envoy, Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura, that Cuba agreed to the asylum request as a humanitarian gesture.
"Our acceptance on this issue is from a humanitarian point of view. Cuba is not a country to take in terrorism," the sources quoted Castro as saying.

Thursday's announcement formalises a promise Castro made earlier this month to Peru President Alberto Fujimori in Havana. The Cuban leader said it was a "moral duty" to take in the rebels if they wanted asylum.
Following Fujimori's trip to Havana, the rebels told reporters they wanted to stay in Peru but said they reserved comment on the possibility of asylum in Cuba.
Komura was to travel on Thursday afternoon to the Dominican Republic, which is also believed to be willing to offer asylum for some of the MRTA members.
Despite the diplomatic moves, the MRTA has given no indication it will accept asylum or end its siege with anything less than the release of its jailed members.
Komura arrived in Havana following a two-day visit to Lima, where he urged Fujimori to push for fresh talks with the rebels. The sides have met only once in the last two weeks.
Despite Japan's pressure for dialogue, accusations of human rights abuses by the Peruvian army threatened to further delay the resumption of talks.
A leading Peruvian human rights group said the army arrested and tortured dozens of innocent peasants in an operation to flush MRTA members out of their strongholds in the central jungle.
APRODEH said the army detained 38 villagers, including seven children, in the town of Alto Yurinaki, about 200 miles (320 km) east of Lima, during an offensive on March 9.
Peru's military says the arrest of 38 "MRTA terrorists" thwarted a planned attack on a military base in the area.
But a senior MRTA rebel in the jungle told Reuters the army detained villagers who "have nothing to do with the movement."
In exchange for their hostages, the rebels want the release of more than 300 jailed comrades and about 100 more prisoners they claim are falsely convicted on terrorism charges.
With the talks stalled over these demands, a three-man mediating panel was working to persuade the sides to grant some concesssions.

"This is the time to understand that there is a margin for a peaceful solution but it is attainable only through pardon and reconciliation," the Vatican's mediator, Peruvian Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, said on Wednesday.
His appeal coincided with a Kyodo news report that Fujimori was ready to make "a certain compromise" involving pardons for some rebels jailed with excessive sentences.
